government.narrative: India is a federal parliamentary republic.{{9}} The President is the constitutional head of state, and executive power sits with the Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers, who answer to Parliament.{{9}} Narendra Modi has been Prime Minister since 2014 and began a third term in June 2024, and Droupadi Murmu has been President since July 2022.{{8}}{{9}} For health, the key feature is the constitutional division of powers. Entry 6 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule, 'public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries', makes health care delivery a state responsibility.{{1}}{{2}} Education, including medical education, sits on the Concurrent List, where Union law prevails when the two conflict.{{1}} In practice, the Union shapes the system through money and regulation. It funds and designs flagship schemes such as the National Health Mission and Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, it regulates medical education through the National Medical Commission, and it steers state priorities through Finance Commission grants.{{3}} The Fifteenth Finance Commission, for example, earmarked about Rs 70,051 crore in health grants through local governments for FY2021-22 to FY2025-26.{{3}} States still decide whether and how to take part. Odisha and Delhi joined PM-JAY only in 2025, and West Bengal signed on in June 2026, which completed nationwide rollout.{{4}}{{5}}{{6}} Several states also run their own insurance schemes alongside it. For a foreign partner, this means the relevant counterparty is often a state government rather than New Delhi. Cleveland Clinic's June 2026 MediCity memorandum, for instance, was signed with the Government of Maharashtra.{{7}} Regulation, land allocation, scheme empanelment and public-hospital collaboration all vary state by state, so market entry needs to be planned at state level.

financing.narrative: India spends little on health relative to its income, and households still pay a large share directly. The tenth round of National Health Accounts, covering 2022-23 and released in May 2026, puts total health expenditure at 3.37 percent of GDP on the new GDP series, or Rs 6,373 per person.{{1}}{{2}}{{3}} Government spending reached 1.48 percent of GDP on the same series.{{1}} On the old 2011-12 series the two ratios are 3.28 and 1.43 percent.{{1}}{{4}} Either way, government spending is far short of the 2.5 percent target set by the National Health Policy 2017 for 2025.{{9}} Over the decade the trend has been positive: the government share of total spending rose from 28.6 percent in 2013-14 to 43.7 percent, and the out-of-pocket share fell from 64.2 percent to 43.4 percent.{{2}} In 2022-23, however, the trend reversed.{{3}} The previous NHA round had shown a COVID-era peak for 2021-22, with a 48 percent government share and out-of-pocket spending of only 39.4 percent.{{5}}{{2}} When emergency pandemic spending ended, households again picked up a larger part of the bill.{{3}} Insurance is spreading. The NSO's 2025 survey found health insurance coverage of 47.4 percent in rural areas and 44.3 percent in urban areas, up from 14.1 and 19.1 percent in 2017-18.{{7}}{{8}} Coverage is mainly through PM-JAY and state schemes, and it has not yet brought down out-of-pocket spending, which still averages Rs 34,064 per hospitalisation excluding childbirth, and Rs 50,508 in private hospitals.{{7}}{{8}} Union health spending continues to rise, with the 2026-27 budget up nearly 10 percent over the previous year's revised estimate.{{6}} For a foreign partner, the financing picture points to a two-tier market. A price-sensitive mass market is anchored by PM-JAY rates, and a smaller cash-paying and privately insured segment, together with inbound international patients, sustains premium tertiary care.

workforce.narrative: India's health workforce is growing but remains thin and unevenly distributed. The Health Ministry told Parliament in December 2025 that 13.88 lakh allopathic doctors were registered.{{1}}{{3}} That is fewer than one registered doctor per 1,000 people, and fewer still are actually practising.{{1}} The government's headline ratio of one doctor per 811 people is reached only by adding 7.5 lakh AYUSH (traditional medicine) practitioners and assuming 80 percent of all registrants are active.{{1}}{{3}} On nursing, a July 2026 reply to the Rajya Sabha reported 46.02 lakh registered nursing personnel as of December 2025, or 2.60 per 1,000.{{4}} Of these, 34.88 lakh were registered nurses and midwives and 10.59 lakh were auxiliary nurse midwives.{{4}} Only 14.24 lakh are enrolled in the national Nurses Registration and Tracking System, so the number actually working in India, rather than inactive or abroad, is uncertain.{{5}} Even on generous counts, India's combined density of doctors, nurses and midwives is below WHO's threshold of 4.45 per 1,000 and a fraction of OECD averages of roughly 4 doctors and 9 nurses per 1,000.{{4}}{{7}}{{8}}{{9}} Beds are a similar constraint: the 8.19 lakh beds in public facilities counted in March 2023 amount to fewer than 0.6 per 1,000 people.{{6}} Shortages are worst in the populous northern states, while specialists cluster in metro private hospitals.{{4}} The Union Budget 2026-27 targets the allied-health gap with a plan to add 1 lakh allied health professionals over five years across ten disciplines, including radiology, anaesthesia and operating-theatre technology, and to train 1.5 lakh caregivers.{{11}}{{12}}{{13}} For a foreign academic partner, workforce development is one of the clearest openings, including nursing excellence programs, sub-specialty fellowships, allied-health training and hospital leadership education.

recent_developments.headline: Union Budget 2026-27 raises health allocation nearly 10% and backs five regional medical hubs
recent_developments.summary: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare received Rs 1,06,530.42 crore, nearly 10 percent above the previous year's revised estimate.{{1}} Allocations included Rs 39,390 crore for the National Health Mission, Rs 9,500 crore for PM-JAY and Rs 4,770 crore for PM-ABHIM.{{1}} The budget also announced a scheme for five regional medical hubs, developed with states and the private sector, combining care, education and research, along with plans to add 1 lakh allied health professionals and train 1.5 lakh caregivers.{{1}}{{2}} The hubs are intended to strengthen India's position in medical value travel.{{2}}

recent_developments.headline: NEET-UG 2026 cancelled over a question-paper leak; re-examination held on 21 June
recent_developments.summary: The National Testing Agency cancelled the NEET-UG examination held on 3 May 2026 for more than 22 lakh candidates after investigators found that questions had leaked in advance, and the case was handed to the Central Bureau of Investigation.{{1}} Nearly 20 lakh candidates sat the re-examination on 21 June 2026, and results were declared on 16 July 2026, with 11.21 lakh qualifying.{{2}}{{3}}{{1}} It was the second NEET integrity crisis in three years, a relevant consideration for any foreign partner relying on India's national admissions and licensing system.{{1}}

recent_developments.headline: West Bengal joins Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, completing nationwide rollout
recent_developments.summary: West Bengal signed an MoU with the National Health Authority at a ceremony presided over by Union Health Minister J P Nadda, in the presence of Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari.{{1}}{{3}} It became the 36th state or union territory to implement PM-JAY, the last to do so.{{1}}{{2}} About 1.24 crore eligible families in the state gain up to Rs 5 lakh a year in hospital cover.{{1}} Including families of ASHAs, anganwadi workers and helpers, and senior citizens aged 70 and over, the beneficiary base is about 1.43 crore families.{{1}}

recent_developments.headline: Maharashtra signs MoU with Cleveland Clinic, Brookfield and Arodhan Health City for Navi Mumbai International MediCity
recent_developments.summary: The Government of Maharashtra signed an MoU at Cleveland Clinic's headquarters in Cleveland with Cleveland Clinic, Brookfield Asset Management and Arodhan Health City to develop Navi Mumbai International MediCity, with Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis joining by video.{{1}}{{2}}{{3}}{{4}} The planned 250-acre healthcare, research, medical education and medical tourism hub, next to the new Navi Mumbai airport, has expected investment of about US$1.2 billion and more than 10,000 jobs.{{1}}{{3}}{{4}} Cleveland Clinic is named as anchor institution, and CEO Tom Mihaljevic said in the state's announcement that it would contribute its expertise to the ecosystem.{{1}}{{4}} Cleveland Clinic has not issued its own release, and the project is at MoU stage.

recent_developments.headline: Manipal Health Enterprises lists after Rs 9,275 crore IPO
recent_developments.summary: Manipal Health Enterprises, which reports 49 hospitals and 13,037 licensed beds across 14 states and union territories as of 31 March 2026, listed on the NSE and BSE at about an 11 percent premium to its Rs 590 issue price.{{1}}{{2}}{{3}} The IPO was subscribed nearly five times, led by qualified institutional buyers.{{1}} Manipal grew from 33 hospitals and 9,520 beds in March 2024, mainly through acquisitions of AMRI, Medica and Sahyadri, and cites a CRISIL report describing it as the largest pan-India multispecialty network by bed capacity.{{3}}

recent_developments.headline: KKR agrees to acquire Medicover India as Sweden's Medicover exits Indian hospitals
recent_developments.summary: KKR signed definitive agreements to acquire Medicover India, a network of 24 hospitals with about 4,800 beds across South and West India.{{1}} Medicover said the transaction values Medicover Hospitals India at EUR 1.2 billion, about US$1.4 billion, and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals; KKR did not disclose terms.{{2}}{{1}} The seller, Swedish healthcare group Medicover, is leaving the Indian hospital market to focus on Poland, Germany and Romania.{{2}}{{3}} The deal is a further sign of global private equity driving hospital consolidation in India.

recent_developments.headline: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY marks eight years with 13.25 crore funded hospital admissions
recent_developments.summary: On the scheme's eighth anniversary, Union Health Minister J P Nadda and the National Health Authority reported that PM-JAY had funded 13.25 crore hospital admissions worth Rs 2.03 lakh crore through more than 38,000 empanelled public and private hospitals.{{1}}{{2}} About 48.5 crore Ayushman cards have been issued, and more than 12 crore families have Rs 5 lakh in annual cover across 1,961 procedures in 27 specialties.{{1}}{{2}}{{3}}

resolution_log: MSK and iCliniq: removed the claim that the MSK India pages remain live. Every mskcc.icliniq.com URL now returns HTTP 410 ('permanently removed'), which I confirmed myself. The text now states the confirmed 2 August 2021 launch (PR Newswire release, opened) and says current status is unknown and the program may have ended. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

GDP (PPP): replaced the stale US$16.2 trillion and US$11,159 per capita (2024) with the current World Bank series, US$17.2 trillion and US$11,748 per capita for 2025, keeping 2024 values of US$15.6 trillion and US$10,719. I queried the World Bank API myself (last updated 13 July 2026). Removed the Trading Economics source. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

Urban population: corrected 36.9% (2024) to 35.7% (2025), with 35.4% for 2024, per the World Bank API, which I queried myself. The narrative's 'about 37 percent' became 'about 36 percent in 2025'. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

Johns Hopkins and IIT Bombay: corrected the agreement year from 2025 to 9 February 2023. The '2025' came from the page's URL folder. JHU sites block automated fetches, so I confirmed the date through the institute's indexed pages, and all three verifiers agree. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

US tariffs: rewrote the sequence. Trump announced the deal on 2 February 2026; the joint statement is dated 6 February (White House, opened). The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 February (Akashvani, opened), a 10% Section 122 tariff followed from 24 February, and a 10% Section 301 duty has applied to India since 24 July 2026 (Morgan Lewis, opened). The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act was signed on 18 September 2026 (Baker McKenzie, opened). The verifiers' correct versions differed on the current regime; I adopted V3's Section 301 version after confirming it. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

Mayo and AIG: V1 said membership was 'probably active', while V2 and V3 could not check it. I confirmed the October 2019 joining (Mayo release on Newswise) and that the Post Bulletin (February 2025) cites 2023 tax filings listing India among member locations. AIG's own Mayo page returns 404 and Mayo's member list blocks fetches. The text now states what is confirmed and says present membership is not confirmed, without calling it active. Raised by V1.

Mayo and Lilavati: widened the scope from nursing alone to the January 2025 announcement, which also covered a 300-bed cancer institute and a GIFT City project (Medical Buyer/PTI, opened). Removed the past tense 'ran'. The text says those projects are described only by Lilavati's trustees, that Mayo did not answer press questions (Post Bulletin, opened), and that their status is unknown. Raised by V1.

Mayo and Adani: removed the 'strictly advisory, not a joint venture' spokesperson quote. It appears only in a Star Tribune search snippet, and the article could not be opened. Mayo's role is now described from Adani's own 10 February 2025 release, which I opened. Found in my own check.

Mayo Mumbai office: removed the unsupported word 'active'. The office is now dated to its February 2023 opening (Mayo release on Newswise, opened), and the Mumbai subsidiary named in Mayo's filings was added. Found in my own check.

Max Healthcare: corrected 5,257 operational beds to 4,966 at 31 March 2026 (Business Standard, InvestyWise), plus the 10,000-bed FY2030 target. The cited Whalesbook source never gave 5,257. Raised by V1.

MD Anderson and Tata Memorial: replaced 'current formal status is not confirmed'. MD Anderson's own ECHO-PACA II page, which I opened, lists Tata Memorial Hospital under a Sister Institution Network Fund grant. Confirmed the 6 October 2003 signing (India Herald, opened). Dropped the SACT 2025 joint-session reference because the only source is a December 2024 social post announcing it. Raised by V2; V1 and V3 had it in could_not_check.

UPMC: changed 'historical' to 'no current India activity found', since absence from a location list does not show the agreement ended. Added the earlier Citizens Hospital, Hyderabad pathology-lab work. Checked against the EurekAlert release and the UPMC locations page, both opened. Raised by V2.
NewYork-Presbyterian: added dates, Ahmedabad in November 2007 and Mumbai from October to November 2008, from the NYP release, which I opened. Raised by V1+V2.

UCLA: reframed as department-level, grant-funded OB/GYN (GRACE) projects: the Narendra Modi Medical College exchange (2024 pilot, seminars from summer 2025) and the completed first phase of the AIIMS postpartum-haemorrhage project. Confirmed on UCLA's page, which I opened. Raised by V1.

Mount Sinai and Ramaiah: added the omitted July 2024 exclusive long-term collaboration. Confirmed with Mount Sinai Press Office's GlobeNewswire release of 12 July 2024 (opened via Yahoo Finance), Deccan Herald on the 10-year term from 1 July 2024 (opened), and Ramaiah's collaborations page, which still presents the partnership (opened). Current activity is not asserted beyond that. Raised by V3.

Johns Hopkins and HCL: no verifier could check this. JHMI's own page, via its indexed text, describes a 10-year affiliation from February 2014, and a 2014 Domain-b report (opened) confirms the tie-up. The text states the term would have ended in 2024 and that no renewal or current activity could be confirmed. From the could_not_check lists of V1+V2+V3.

Cleveland Clinic MediCity: confirmed the 10 June 2026 MoU, the parties, the 250 acres, US$1.2 billion and 10,000 jobs, and the Mihaljevic quote through the state's announcement as carried by Free Press Journal and India TV, both opened. Cleveland Clinic's newsroom has no release, so the text now says so. Confirmed the in-country representative on Cleveland Clinic's India page. Found in my own check.

NCD premature mortality: corrected 22% (2019) to 23.6% (2021), with 23.7% for 2019, from the WHO Global Health Observatory API (NCDMORT3070), which I queried myself. Updated the narrative to match. Raised by V3.

SRS indicators: updated to the SRS Statistical Report 2024 (released May 2026): TFR 1.9 (2024), IMR 24 (2024), Bihar 2.9 and Delhi 1.2. Replaced '18 states and UTs below 2.1' with 'all states except six in the north', per The Wire and Business Standard, both opened. Raised by V2+V3.

National Health Accounts: made the GDP series consistent. THE is 3.37% on the new series and 3.28% on the old; GHE is 1.48% on the new series and 1.43% on the old. I checked this against the NHA 2022-23 report text. Raised by V2+V3.

Government hospital beds: the three verifiers disagreed. V1 attributed the 0.79 figure to Knight Frank, V2 to National Health Profile data, and V3 to beds as of 31 March 2021. I opened the source chain: Knight Frank's number is actually a 1.3 total-bed ratio, and the official figure is 8,18,661 public beds as of 31 March 2023 (PIB Rajya Sabha reply, Health Dynamics of India 2022-23). That works out to fewer than 0.6 per 1,000, and the 0.79 figure cannot be reproduced from official data. Replaced it with the official count and removed the unsourced '2.7 global average'. Raised by V1+V2+V3.

Postgraduate seats: added the official 82,059 total that the Health Minister gave Parliament in December 2025 (Deccan Herald, opened), with the roughly 57,500 NMC matrix figure presented as a narrower MD/MS count. Raised by V1+V2.

NEET-UG 2026: added the cancellation of the 3 May sitting on 12 May over a paper leak, the CBI probe, and the fact that 21 June was a re-examination. Confirmed on Wikipedia and in the NTA result notice. Added a matching recent-development entry. Raised by V1+V3.
Pharma exports: changed 'about a third to the US' to about US$9.5 billion (roughly 30%), down nearly 10% year on year, with a total of US$31.1 billion (Business Standard, opened). Raised by V1.
GDP: added Q1 FY2026-27 real growth of 7.8% from the MoSPI press note of 31 August 2026, which I opened. Raised by V2.

West Bengal PM-JAY: split the families into 1.24 crore eligible and about 1.43 crore including ASHA, anganwadi and 70+ families (PIB, opened). Removed the unconfirmed Vigyan Bhavan venue. Raised by V2+V3; V1 had the venue in could_not_check.
Out-of-pocket costs: added the 'excluding childbirth' qualifier and the private-hospital average of Rs 50,508 (median Rs 24,000 against Rs 1,100), from the NSS press note text. Raised by V2.

IHH and Fortis: corrected the implication that the open offer raised IHH's stake. IHH has held about 31.17% since 2018, and only 1,778 shares were tendered (InvestyWise BSE summary, opened). Raised by V2+V3.

KKR and Medicover: attributed the EUR 1.2 billion (about US$1.4 billion) valuation and Q4 2026 closing to Medicover's own release, which I opened, and noted that KKR did not disclose terms. Raised by V2+V3.

Medical arrivals: changed 'reached 6.44 lakh' to show the decline from 6.59 lakh (2023) and 6.97 lakh (2019) (DD News, opened). Confirmed the 2024 source-country ranking led by Bangladesh at about 4.8 lakh via InsightsIAS, citing Bureau of Immigration data. Raised by V3; the ranking was in the could_not_check lists of V1+V2+V3.

MBBS seats: dated the matrix to September 2026. Replaced the unverified 2024 baseline of 1,17,750 with the official 1,28,875 UG seats reported to Parliament in December 2025. Manipal IPO: removed 'second-largest Indian IPO of 2026', which is unsupported, and changed 4.92 times to 'nearly five times' per Business Standard. Added the 33-hospital 2024 baseline from Groww's DRHP summary. From V3's could_not_check.
